title: Async decommit queue backpressure causing slab bloat in KV-heavy workloads
creator: Asha Patel
description: When serving workloads with aggressive continuous batching and large KV cache residency, we observe steady GPU memory growth that is not reclaimed promptly by the allocator. Initial signals point to backpressure on the cudaMallocAsync decommit path: many small transient allocations are enqueued for async decommit on streams that are not synchronizing fast enough, causing the slab pool's residency to grow and producing fragmentation. This ticket captures investigation, repro, experiments, and proposed mitigations for allocator-level backpressure and KV cache interaction.
repro_steps:
1) Deploy bench server with KV cache enabled and config: kv_eviction_policy=LRU, kv_prefetch=true.
2) Use continuous batching load generator with distribution: 80% short sequences (<=64 tokens), 20% long (512+), interarrival 5-20ms to mimic PLG traffic.
3) Track: nvidia-smi, runtime allocator traces (alloc/free ops with timestamps), and slab residency metrics from debug knobs.
4) Observe sustained resident growth after ~30 minutes, GPU memory delta ~20-50MB/min under default settings.
5) Toggle ALLOC_FALLBACK=cudaMalloc to compare (sync path) and observe immediate reduction in growth but higher tail latency.
(See attached dashboard links for exact bench commands.)
investigation_notes:
- Timeline: started from customer report of gradual OOM on heavy chat routing. Correlated with increased KV cache hit churn and a new batching policy rolled out last week.
- Traces show decommit queue backlog on several CUDA streams; cudaFreeAsync semantics delayed until stream drain which isn't happening quickly because continuous batching keeps appending work.
- Slab allocator keeps pages resident because decommit callbacks are deferred; small allocations (~4KB-64KB) dominate and don't coalesce, causing internal fragmentation.
- Switching to synchronous malloc/free immediately reduces residency but increases median latency by ~6-12ms on our benchmark.
- Notably, using a per-request temporary stream (then synchronize) also clears the backlog but increases CPU overhead and harms throughput.
- Instrumentation gaps: we need per-stream decommit queue length and timestamped nvtx markers for decommit events to verify exact delay distribution.
experiments: E1: Enable aggressive eager decommit for small bins (threshold=32KB) - reduced growth by ~40% on bench, small latency impact on 99th percentile.
E2: Add decommit draining background thread that issues explicit streamSync on low-priority worker streams - cleared backlog but increased CPU usage and occasional microstalls.
E3: Coalesce small KV allocations into slab-backed arenas (pre-aggregation) - significantly reduced fragmentation; requires KV cache change to emit grouped allocations.
E4: Fallback to synchronous cudaMalloc for top-5 hot models as temporary mitigation - effective but not acceptable long-term for latency-sensitive tiers.
proposed_fixes: P1: Implement allocator-side decommit-drain policy: if the async decommit queue length > N or oldest entry age > T, trigger a bounded streamSync/decommit cycle. Configurable per-customer tier.
P2: Add small-allocation coalescing for KV cache-backed buffers: allocate contiguous slab pages aligned to 64KB to reduce fragmentation and make async frees coarser-grained.
P3: Expose allocator telemetry (decommit_queue_length, avg_decommit_latency, per-bin fragmentation) to Console and runtime dashboards for alerting.
P4: Short-term: automatic model-level fallback to sync-malloc when memory growth crosses threshold; rollback to async when stable.
risks_and_tradeoffs:
- Aggressive streamSync causes CPU stalls and higher tail latencies; need careful bounding to avoid user-visible regressions.
- Coalescing reduces fragmentation but may increase peak resident memory due to internal rounding; requires experiments with slab sizing.
- Telemetry adds overhead; keep sampling rate and cardinality low.
- Fallback policies must be tested under mixed-tenant workloads to avoid noisy neighbor effects.
